I've always been highly sceptical of Nuclear Energy. I mean, I'm a Physics UG, I understand the fundamentals of Nuclear Physics, and how one can exploit it to extract heat energy from nuclear fission/fusion, but I've never seen how they add up in a positive way for energy solutions.

For Nuclear Fission...

  • Produces large amounts of radioactive waste that lasts from a few days to thousands of years. So the waste lasts super long and is very very costly to manage and store.

  • Uses Uranium which is already almost all used up on Earth (it's incredibly rare in the Earth's crust). So the fuel is already limited.

  • The radioactivity of the fuel in the reactor wears away the surrounding casings, such as the moderators and what not, and so everything has to be completely overhauled eventually. Fission power plants don't last very long.

  • Plants are very expensive to build.

  • And lots of other negatives, which I've never seen outweighed by the VERY few positives. Heck, "no emissions" isn't even a positive, because it isn't true. The building and running and decommisioning of plants ends up produces huge amounts of emissions.

For Nuclear Fusion...

  • Very costly plant to build (complexity), and requires highly-skilled work force so very costly to run.

  • We still can't even get energy out of fusion.

  • Fusion releases huge amounts of neutrons and stuff which fly out and corrode the inner surfaces of the reactor. Similar problem to nuclear fission plants. Things have to be replaced very often.

  • Fusion, if we get it to work, would probably be atleast a better idea than fission, as an energy solution.

All in all, it's solar power all the way, until fusion power plants can be realised.

And even then, it's only until the water lasts. Fusion plants use processed water as fuel (I believe), and although it isn't exactly highly limited, water on Earth is finite. And greenhouse gases, which continue to be emitted, will accelerate the depletion of water on Earth.

SO...

In the end, it's going to Mars or something, extracting water from the ground and using crazy advanced ISRU and habitat tech to survive long term.

So this morning I went to breakfast and ordered a cup of coffee and a glass of water. The water came out in a tiny cup. It was basically a toddler cup. At best it held four sips of water. This seems to be a thing at some restaurants. Drinks like Coke or tea come in a normal glass, but water comes in this ridiculous tiny cup. Can someone who works in food service explain to me why you do this.
Why do restaurants give you tiny glasses of water?
I don't work there, and this is just speculation: That might have been one of those tiny cups of water that you get with espresso and for some reason the waiter thought you wanted one of those.

I don't think it was that. I have been to this restaurant before and they always give you water in a tiny cup. A few other restaurants I've been to do it as well (Denny's comes to mind). It seems like there is a company policy to give you a tiny little cup of water.
I'd assume they give you a small cup to encourage you to purchase a drink.
So you have to buy their overpriced sodas?

Most places restaurants can't charge you for tap water. So smaller paper cups are cheaper than larger ones. Also the fact if you decide to refill the water cup with "sprite" they lose less in the theft.

In these places, I just buck up and say "Hey, I'm willing to pay for the cost of a drink, I just want a real cup of water. I'm not a child." And they usually just give me the large cup for free. It's embarrassing to have to ask, but just be bold but respectful about it. The server wants your tip.

If you're eating at a restaurant you can often ask for a jug of water.

Then you either get plenty or get to see a really cute tiny jug.

In some states, restaurants have to serve you tap water for free. They can't charge for it. So they make it as inconvenient as possible for the customer. The objective is not to lower their costs (smaller cups cost almost as much as large cups, and a small cup's worth of tap water costs almost as much as a large cup's worth) but customers will order more beverages if drinking the free water is inconvenient.
